posts.author: Dutchelm05
posts.content_md:
OK first reading this from Richard Rallison on how DCG got started made my heart race. A demented mind at work 

But the part were he says he accidentally dropped an exposed plate into hardening fixer for 30 seconds blew me away. I don't think Oliver Stone could even make such a movie! The one area that caught my attention was "My method of controlling the color and clarity of master holograms was not disclosed til 1985. I dropped a developed broadband hologram into a certain bath that was about 75% alcohol and when I retrieved it and dipped it in hot dry alcohol it came back as a low scatter blue hologram." 

Is this true? Will it go narrowband and be good enough for a master?

The History of Dichromates

Richard D. Rallison, Ralcon Development Lab

1.3 Serendipity

Back to the story, I returned to Hughes with one of Mike's broken 8 x10 inch dichromates determined to produce my own, Mike was not about to share more of his tricks of the trade so I was on my own. I coated Knox unflavored gelatin "Jello" on glass plates in my apartment using a record player built into an old steamer trunk. The dichromate processes described in the literature by Shankoff, Lin and Chang were all too time consuming to suit me. Mike had suggested during a phone conversation that I mix in all the sensitizing dichromate before coating to save some time and that helped. Everything I made initially came out milky white until I accidentally dropped an exposed plate into Milton's hardening fixer prior to soaking it in water. It was only in the fixer for 30 seconds but that proved to be sufficient to harden it enough to take the shock of hot alcohol without precipitation. A short process was immediately at hand. From then on I could make coatings on any glass surface in 5 minutes, expose them in another 5 minutes, process them in another 5 minutes and seal them up in less than 5 minutes. I immediately produced a few boxes full for show and tell and then lit the lab on fire. I managed to keep that trick under my hat until 1982, when Fred Unterseher persuaded me to publish it. I inadvertently also sold it to Steve McGrew (Holosonics) in 1979 and thought he might make it public just as I was selling it to IBM, but he never did publish. What he did publish was a very fine paper on color control in DCG in 1980, one of the first papers useful to artists working in color at the time. My method of controlling the color and clarity of master holograms was not disclosed til 1985. I dropped a developed broadband hologram into a certain bath that was about 75% alcohol and when I retrieved it and dipped it in hot dry alcohol it came back as a low scatter blue hologram. From that day in Nov 1975 I had a fast, tunable way to make bright masters that added almost no noise to the copies and so I finally had all the processes I needed to start making masters and churning out thousands of bright "dichromates" for sale. Which is what I did. 

[http://alt.xmission.com/~ralcon/dichrohist.html](http://alt.xmission.com/~ralcon/dichrohist.html)

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Is this true? Will it go narrowband and be good enough for a master?

Yuppers. A reprocessed hologram definitely shifts blue, get cleaner and narrower. You can even reprocess a second time if the first time does not work well enough. And by using alcohol a little less then 75% you can control the shift. If 75% give you blue, 65 may give you green and 50 may give you gold. As you use a lower concentration you leave some of the broadband and dont shift blue as much.

What really gets me, and it would put me back into the lab is this statement.

"From then on I could make coatings on any glass surface in 5 minutes, expose them in another 5 minutes, process them in another 5 minutes and seal them up in less than 5 minutes."

I guess I have always thought of DCG to be so particular that I never tried a speedy method. Obviously the plate is going to be real young at 5 minutes. So how did he get the coating dry enough to be exposed and processed in 5 minutes? It seems in 5 minutes the gel would ooze off the glass if held vertically. Did he bake or stretch the truth on the time to cure I wonder? He states he used Knox, so that's about 220 bloom, not to terribly high. Anyway it definitely seems worth investigating.

My biggest downfall is all the prep time it takes to make the film. If I could make just a couple plates at a time and expose right away, WOW!

I think I may follow up on this "quick" method.

Use young film, get a nice white milky hologram and repocess. 

Hey Tony, thank for sharing that! If I get into the to give this a whirl, I will post my results.

posts.author: Dutchelm05
posts.content_md:
Hey John,

Here is what I think is going on. Richard used a spin method (you should still have that 78 RPM motor I sent you). I think he used small disc like the size of pendents. I think if you drop some dichromate on it and allowed to spin for a bit, maybe apply some heat from a blow dryer (not too much) the plate will be dry in no time. The reason why I say this is 20+ years ago, that's how I did it (except I used a 120rpm motor and one even faster but the plates would fly everywhere ), but larger plates were more difficult. Of coarse back then I did not accidentally drop my plate in Fixer!!! But small stuff is easy and would not take long to dry.

I know many of us would love to see you back in the lab John!

Later

Yea, I remember reading somewhere that someone uses the technique of drying while air is blowing on the plate. Like you said, not too hard and not to hot, just a nice warm flow. Probably mount the dryer a 2 feet or so away from plate and put it on low. 

I was thinking of using the veil/spin. I don't really want to go smaller then 4x5.

Did you have any luck coating 4x5's with just the spin method (probably heat the gelatin a little hotter and spin a little faster)?

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: My notes from working with Rallison's method while at Portson Holographics in Kansas in 1990 includes a heat lamp placed over the spin coater, at a height and distance from the center determined by trial and error. I think we put a puddle in the center of the plate, spun it out, and let it spin for a short time while it dried.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Thanks BobH. What is your opinion on spinning larger plates with the puddle method while increasing emulsion temp a llittle and increasing RPM's a little? Any insite. I know it will have to be finalized by trial and error, but any recollection would be helpful.

We used to spin resist at close to 10k rpm and needed to ramp up to the rmp in a very short time. Of couse that only gave us a couple of microns in thickness and resist is more fluid then Gelatin. And we had to enclose the spinner and plate in bullet proof plexiglass. I know that is extreem of course for DCG.
